title: Wyandanch
summary: Wyandanch (died 1659) was a Montaukett sachem whose family alliances, diplomacy across Long Island Sound, and land and shoreline agreements shaped seventeenth-century Long Island. His life connects Montauk, the Gardiners, neighboring Native leaders, and the continuing leadership of his wife and children.
content:
A Montaukett life across Long Island Sound

Wyandanch (also written Wyandance, Wayandanch, and Wiantause) was a Montaukett sachem who died in 1659. Over more than two decades, he negotiated with Native leaders and English officials from Montauk to Hempstead and across Long Island Sound. The surviving record brings him into view during the Pequot War in 1637: a leader seeking security for his people, a father working to recover captives, and a negotiator whose agreements helped reshape Long Island’s landholding.1 2 4

Historian John A. Strong describes Wyandanch as an alliance sachem whose influence depended on family relationships and negotiation. Neighboring Native leaders retained their own interests even when English buyers sought his confirmation.12

Family, homeland, and inherited connections

Wyandanch’s home was Montauk, at Long Island’s eastern end. His older brother Poggatacut led the Manhansett of Shelter Island. The 1648 East Hampton agreement names them alongside Momoweta of Corchaug and Nowedonah of Shinnecock. These leaders appear together in negotiations that crossed the bays and the Sound.1 3

His wife, Wuchikittawbut, and their son Wyancombone—whose name appears in several spellings—held a place in the family’s political and landholding affairs. Both marked the July 14, 1659 deed with him. His daughter Quashawam later exercised leadership and defended family land interests in her own right.1 7

Family memory also connected Wyandanch to the western North Shore. In testimony recorded in 1666, his former chief counselor Pauquatoun said that Wyandanch’s grandmother had lived on Cattawamnuck land. Quashawam described kinship among her parents, Tackapousha, and other sachems with interests there, explaining that relatives were to receive part of the payment. Her account makes the family relationships behind the deeds visible.7

1637: Peace and trade under the shadow of war

Following the English attack on the Pequot fort at Mystic in May 1637, Wyandanch visited Fort Saybrook, at the mouth of the Connecticut River. Lion Gardiner, the fort’s commander, later recalled that Wyandanch asked whether the English were angry with all Native people and whether Long Islanders could trade with them.1

Gardiner’s answer made access to trade depend on violence against Pequot refugees. He demanded the killing of Pequots who reached Long Island and the delivery of their heads. Wyandanch said he would consult his older brother; Gardiner then recorded receiving heads in several deliveries. Their long alliance began within this brutal wartime bargain. Gardiner wrote his account in 1660, more than twenty years after the encounter.1

1644–1649: Alliances and the first East Hampton agreement

In September 1644, the United Colonies commissioners at Hartford issued a certificate naming Youghco, Wiantause, Moughmaitow, and Weenagaminin. It recorded their declared friendship with both English and Dutch settlers, acknowledged an English tributary relationship, and required satisfaction for injuries attributed to their people. Youghco requested the certificate; its language shows the conditions colonial authorities attached to peace.2

On April 29, 1648, Wyandanch joined Poggatacut, Momoweta, and Nowedonah in the agreement through which English settlers acquired East Hampton land between Southampton and Napeague. The goods listed included coats, mirrors, hoes, hatchets, and knives. Cockenoe, recorded as Chectanoo, marked it as interpreter.3

The agreement also reserved continuing Native uses of the landscape: fishing in creeks and ponds, hunting in the woods, gathering shells for wampum, and receiving the fins and tails of stranded whales. A further provision divided a deer driven into the water and killed by an English person: the body went to the English hunter and the skin to the sachem. These were specific rights within a working homeland.3

During a late-1640s Southampton crisis following the killing of an English woman, Wyandanch helped negotiate the delivery of accused men to colonial authorities. Gardiner recalled remaining among the Montauketts as a personal guarantee while Wyandanch went to Southampton. Later testimony by Thomas Halsey and Thomas Sayre described Mandush acknowledging a relationship with Wyandanch through a ceremony involving earth and gestures of recognition. English officials subsequently invoked that relationship in Shinnecock land transactions.1 9

1651–1654: Leadership, war, and a daughter’s captivity

After Poggatacut’s death in 1651, Wyandanch became increasingly prominent in East End negotiations. Conflict with Ninigret, the Eastern Niantic sachem across the Sound, brought devastating attacks on the Montauketts. Strong dates the capture of Wyandanch’s daughter and other Montaukett people to a raid in 1653.1 10

A letter of September 6, 1654 conveys Wyandanch’s urgency as a father. Writing at his request, East Hampton minister Thomas James told John Winthrop Jr. that Wyandanch feared for his daughter and the other captives, as well as another attack. He asked that ransom wampum reportedly intercepted by Thomas Stanton be forwarded quickly. Recovering the people mattered more to him than losing the payment if the captors failed to keep their word.4

The family’s 1659 deed credited Lion Gardiner’s money and goods with helping them defend themselves and ransom their daughter and friends. That acknowledgment links the rescue directly to the later land agreement. Quashawam’s story continued beyond captivity, through her own leadership, agreements, and testimony.1 7

1655–1657: Grazing, a sea journey, and colonial courts

An April 10, 1655 agreement opened Montauk grazing lands to East Hampton livestock.12

In late August 1656, he sailed with five companions aboard Captain Youngs’s vessel to answer accusations before the United Colonies commissioners. Contrary winds brought them first to Milford, Connecticut, before the hearing at Plymouth. Ninigret’s representative accused him of violence after a peace agreement and involvement in a supposed plot to kill Uncas and other sachems through witchcraft. The commissioners found the poisoning allegation unsupported; testimony about the peace agreement remained disputed. They continued measures against attacks on the Montauketts and deferred his unpaid tribute.2

In 1657, after fires in Southampton, colonial authorities imposed a substantial fine on the Shinnecocks. Wyandanch petitioned for relief. On September 8, the commissioners wrote to Connecticut about a £700 penalty and Wyandanch’s complaint of damage by settlers’ horses. They urged that penalties not exceed the guilt proved against living people. The obligation drew land and diplomacy together: the later Quogue transaction with John Ogden was connected to payment of the Shinnecock fine.2 9

1657–1658: Western connections, boundaries, and Cockenoe’s work

Wyandanch’s agreements reached well beyond Montauk. The June 1, 1657 Huntington deed concerned five necks of South Shore meadowland and specified both immediate goods and an annual coat for six years. Keeossechok, the Secatogue sachem, confirmed his interest. On July 23, both sachems marked a separate half-neck agreement with Jonas Wood. Their paired names preserve the role of the local Native leader.5

On July 4, 1657, Wyandanch participated in confirmation of the earlier Hempstead purchase. The document speaks for people of Massapequa, Mericoke, and Rockaway and records the Montauk sachem’s name as Wantagh. Tackapousha, Cockenoe, and other Native participants also marked it. A May 11, 1658 confirmation described marked trees and boundaries from the North Shore to the South Shore. This is a direct connection to Merrick and the Hempstead Plains.6

At Shelter Island on May 14, 1658, he confirmed a Horse Neck transaction, concerning present-day Lloyd Neck. The August 17 Huntington agreement then named Cockenoe as his agent to deliver three South Shore meadow necks. Cockenoe was to receive separate payment for marking the land; Lion Gardiner was to hold the deed until its conditions were met. Wyandanch and Tackapousha acknowledged payment on May 23, 1659.5

Lion and David Gardiner: friendship, business, and a canoe

Wyandanch’s relationship with the Gardiners ran through everyday work as well as war. A June 10, 1658 beach agreement names Wyandanch, Wyancombone, and associates, with Lion Gardiner as the other party and David Gardiner among the witnesses. It allowed livestock grazing and required an annual payment of twenty-five shillings. Wyandanch retained stranded whales for himself and the Native people entitled to them, together with summer harvesting of flags and bulrushes for mats.3

In the East Hampton court entry dated January 25, 1658/59, Wyandanch sued Jeremy Vaile over damage to his canoe. Lion Gardiner testified about attempts to bring the canoe ashore after his son and Vaile returned. John Rose described repairs in exchange for use of the vessel. The jury awarded Wyandanch ten shillings in damages and court charges. The case reveals a valuable working canoe, shared transport arrangements, and Wyandanch’s ability to pursue compensation in an English court.3

1659: Southold, Plum Island, and Quogue

At Southold on January 30, 1659, Wyandanch asserted family interests in Corchaug land. William Wells’s account records the Corchaug leaders’ silence, rather than their assent.12

An April 27 agreement, dated at Gardiners Island, connected him with Samuel Wyllys of Hartford and Plum Island. Southold’s published records identify the consideration as a coat, a barrel of biscuit, and a hundred “muxes or fish hooks.” This was a distinct North Fork transaction.8

On May 12, Wyandanch and his son entered the Quogue agreement with John Ogden for lands west of Canoe Place toward Peaconock, including the West Woods landscape. Its connection to the Shinnecock fine demonstrates the pressure of colonial debt. Later records directed the annual payment to Wyandanch’s daughter and heir. The agreement’s history therefore includes both the land conveyed and the continuing obligations owed to his family.9

July 1659: the family deed to Gardiner

On July 14, at East Hampton, Wyandanch, his wife, and Wyancombone marked the deed giving Lion Gardiner land between Huntington and Setauket. It named Cow Harbor as a western bound and described the inland reach through a valley. The family explained the gift through Gardiner’s help in danger, advice, and assistance in ransoming captives. Their statement of gratitude sits within a document that also transferred a substantial interest in land.1 7

The land became part of the later Smithtown title history. It involved the Nissequogue country, where Nasseconset and other Native people also asserted interests. The Smithtown records preserve a complaint by Nasseconset that Richard Smith had taken his land, followed by further negotiations. The subsequent dispute shows why a single deed cannot tell this landscape’s entire history.7

On July 28, Wyandanch and Wyancombone made a further whale agreement with Gardiner, naming the consent of the local sachems. For twenty-one years, Gardiner would receive bodies and bones of stranded whales within the specified shore bounds, while Native people retained the fins and tails. A whole whale brought a five-pound payment, with proportions for partial carcasses. David Gardiner again appears as a witness.11

Death and the family’s continuing history

Wyandanch died later in 1659, during a period of severe mortality among Native communities. Gardiner’s 1660 account said that he had been poisoned, but supplied no corroborating evidence or named perpetrator. Gardiner mourned him as a friend and brother.1

His death did not end the family’s role in land agreements. On April 6, 1660, Wyancombone and his mother acknowledged a further conveyance to Gardiner extending to the Nissequogue River. David Gardiner’s October 15, 1664 endorsement then recorded satisfaction from Richard Smith for his interest in the earlier deed. In 1666, Quashawam and Pauquatoun’s statements brought family ancestry and shared Native interests back into the written record.1 7

Wyandanch’s life joins the histories of Montaukett families, neighboring Native nations, colonial courts, and landscapes still known by Indigenous names. Follow Quashawam, Wuchikittawbut, Cockenoe, and Tackapousha to continue the connected histories.

why_this_matters: Wyandanch’s agreements reserved fishing, hunting, whale portions, and plants for making mats even as English settlement expanded. His diplomacy joined the protection of these everyday livelihoods with the safety of his family and community. Following his wife, son, daughter, and neighboring sachems through the same records reveals how landholding depended on family relationships and obligations that continued after his death.
activity_update_summary: Expanded Wyandanch’s life history with family relationships, diplomacy, Gardiner connections, land and whale-rights agreements, and 29 linked Historic Moments.
